title: Classes
summary: Bundle data and behaviour into classes: private members, constructors with initialiser lists, const member functions, static members, destructors and operator overloading.
introduction: A class turns a handful of related variables and the functions that keep them consistent into one type with a name. The compiler then enforces the rules you write: nobody can set a bank balance to a negative number if the only way in is a `withdraw` function that checks. This lesson builds a `BankAccount`, a `Rectangle`, a `Counter` that knows how many instances exist, and a `Money` type that works with `+` and `==`.
learningObjectives: Define a class with private data, public member functions and constructors
Initialise members with a member initialiser list and default member initialisers
Mark member functions const and explain what that guarantees
Overload operators and use C++20's defaulted operator==

blocks.text: Data plus the functions that guard it

Members after `public:` are the interface anyone can use; members after `private:` are visible only inside the class. Keeping data private and exposing behaviour is **encapsulation**: every way to change the object goes through a function that can keep it valid. A **constructor** is a member function with the class's name and no return type; it runs when an object is created and should leave the object in a usable state.

blocks.title: account.cpp
Terminal
blocks.content:
$ g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra account.cpp -o account
$ ./account
Ada: 150
withdraw 500 succeeded: false

items: The part after the colon, `: owner_{std::move(owner)}, balance_{openingBalance}`, is the **member initialiser list**. It constructs each member directly instead of default-constructing it and assigning later. Members are initialised in the order they are declared in the class, whatever order the list uses.
`std::move(owner)` moves the caller's string into the member instead of copying it; the parameter is about to die anyway.
`balance() const` promises not to modify the object. Only `const` member functions can be called on a `const BankAccount`, so mark every getter `const`.
The trailing underscore on `owner_` and `balance_` is a common convention that keeps member names from clashing with parameters.

blocks.text: struct, default values and several constructors

`struct` and `class` are the same thing except that a `struct`'s members are public by default. Use `struct` for plain bundles of data with no invariants and `class` when the data must be protected. A **default member initialiser** (`double width_{1.0};`) gives a member a value whenever a constructor does not mention it, which is the cleanest way to guarantee nothing is left uninitialised.

blocks.title: shapes.cpp

blocks.text: `Point p{3.0, 4.0}` uses **aggregate initialisation**: a struct with public members and no constructors can be filled in declaration order. `explicit` on the one-argument constructor stops the compiler from silently converting a `double` into a `Rectangle`, so `Rectangle r = 4.0;` is rejected while `Rectangle r{4.0};` is fine. Make every single-argument constructor `explicit` unless you specifically want the conversion.

blocks.title: Common mistake: the most vexing parse
blocks.text: `Rectangle unit();` does not create a rectangle. C++ reads it as the declaration of a function named `unit` that takes no parameters and returns a `Rectangle`, and the next line `unit.area()` fails with a confusing error. GCC 11 and later warn: `empty parentheses were disambiguated as a function declaration [-Wvexing-parse]`. Write `Rectangle unit;` or `Rectangle unit{};` instead.

A **destructor** (`~Counter()`) runs automatically when an object's life ends: at the closing brace of its scope, when its container is destroyed, or when the owning smart pointer is reset. That guarantee is the foundation of resource management in C++ and gets its own lesson. A **static** member belongs to the class rather than to any object; there is exactly one `instances_` no matter how many `Counter`s exist.

blocks.title: counter.cpp

blocks.text: `= delete` removes a function the compiler would otherwise generate. The compiler writes a copy constructor, copy assignment, move operations and a destructor for you when you do not; the moment you need to write one of them by hand (because the class owns something), think about all of them. That guideline is known as the *rule of five*, and the easiest way to satisfy it is to own resources only through members that already manage themselves, such as `std::string`, `std::vector` and smart pointers: the *rule of zero*.

Operators are functions with special names, so your types can support `+`, `==` and `<<` just like `int` and `std::string`. Keep the meaning obvious: `+` should add, not append to a log. Since C++20 you can ask the compiler for a memberwise `==` with `= default`, and `!=` comes for free.

blocks.title: money.cpp

blocks.text: `operator<<` is a free function rather than a member because its left operand is the stream, not the `Money`. It returns the stream so that calls chain: `std::cout << total << '\n'`. Storing cents in an integer instead of euros in a `double` is deliberate: binary floating point cannot represent `0.10` exactly, and money should never be rounded by accident.

blocks.title: Headers and source files
blocks.text: In a real project the class definition with its member declarations goes in `account.hpp` and the longer member function bodies in `account.cpp`, written as `double BankAccount::balance() const { ... }`. Short functions defined inside the class body are implicitly `inline`, so a header may contain them.

questions.question: The only difference between `struct` and `class` in C++ is the default access level of their members.
questions.explanation: Members (and base classes) of a `struct` are public by default; those of a `class` are private. Everything else, constructors, member functions, inheritance, works the same.

questions.question: In what order are the members of a class initialised when a constructor runs?
questions.explanation: Members are always initialised in declaration order, regardless of the order in the member initialiser list. Compilers warn (`-Wreorder`) when the list disagrees, because an initialiser that reads another member can otherwise see garbage.
options: In the order written in the member initialiser list
In the order they are declared in the class
